raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan combines valsartan-mediated angiotensin II type-1 receptor blockade with sacubitril-mediated neprilysin inhibition, increasing biologically active natriuretic peptides and other vasoactive substrates while suppressing maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone signaling [1]. The concept followed earlier “vasopeptidase” inhibition: omapatrilat improved some heart-failure and blood-pressure measures but excess angioedema, attributed to simultaneous neprilysin and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition with impaired bradykinin degradation, limited development [2-4]. Sacubitril/valsartan was therefore designed to avoid ACE inhibition and requires a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors.

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is PARADIGM-HF, a rigorously designed, active-controlled trial comparing sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily with enalapril 10 mg twice daily after sequential run-in periods [5]. The trial was stopped early because sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, all-cause mortality, and heart-failure hospitalization [6]. Subsequent analyses showed fewer worsening heart-failure events, less need for treatment intensification, and reductions in sudden death and pump-failure death, suggesting broad disease-modifying benefit rather than only decongestion [7,8]. Benefits were generally preserved across age groups and among patients unable to maintain target doses, supporting use in routine, heterogeneous populations [9,10].

Biomarker data clarify both monitoring and mechanism. Because neprilysin inhibition can increase B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP), which is not a neprilysin substrate, is preferred for assessing response; early and sustained NT-proBNP reductions are prognostically meaningful [11]. BNP may still fall over time, but interpretation shortly after initiation requires caution [27]. Safety in PARADIGM-HF was characterized by more symptomatic hypotension but less renal impairment, hyperkalemia, and cough than enalapril; severe angioedema was uncommon. In patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, sacubitril/valsartan reduced severe hyperkalemia compared with enalapril, potentially facilitating comprehensive neurohormonal therapy [12]. In patients with diabetes, it also modestly improved glycemic control and slowed renal decline in secondary analyses [13,14].

Implementation has shifted from stable outpatient substitution to early initiation after decompensation. In PIONEER-HF, in-hospital initiation after hemodynamic stabilization reduced NT-proBNP more than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [15]. TRANSITION showed that predischarge or early postdischarge initiation was feasible, and TITRATION informed gradual up-titration strategies for patients previously receiving low-dose ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker therapy [16,17]. Reverse-remodeling studies further support early disease modification: PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reduction with improvements in left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction, whereas EVALUATE-HF did not show a significant improvement in aortic characteristic impedance but did demonstrate favorable cardiac remodeling measures [18,19].

In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), evidence is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left atrial reverse remodeling with sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan [20]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but signals favored patients with ejection fraction below the “normal” range and women [21-23]. Renal analyses suggested slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate and fewer renal events, relevant because HFpEF commonly coexists with chronic kidney disease [24]. Contemporary interpretation is that sacubitril/valsartan has strongest evidence in HFrEF, reasonable benefit in selected patients with mildly reduced or lower-range preserved ejection fraction, and less certain value when ejection fraction is clearly normal.

Beyond chronic heart failure, sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or incident heart failure compared with ramipril after acute myocardial infarction in PARADISE-MI, although event patterns were directionally favorable [25]. In advanced HFrEF, LIFE found no significant NT-proBNP advantage over valsartan and highlighted tolerability challenges, emphasizing that very low blood pressure, severe congestion, or end-stage disease may limit initiation [26].

Current guidelines recommend sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, preferably replacing ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker therapy when tolerated, and support selected use across the mildly reduced/preserved spectrum [28,29]. Practical prescribing requires assessment of blood pressure, renal function, potassium, prior angioedema, and concomitant ACE inhibitor exposure; lower starting doses and slower titration are appropriate in frail, hypotensive, or renally impaired patients. Cost-effectiveness analyses generally favor sacubitril/valsartan in eligible HFrEF patients because mortality and hospitalization reductions offset higher drug costs, though affordability remains a real-world barrier [30]. Overall, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition represents one of the major therapeutic advances in modern heart failure, with unequivocal benefit in HFrEF and an evolving, phenotype-dependent role when ejection fraction is higher.
